title: Stack traces, breakpoints, and source maps
hook: A stack trace lists which functions were running when an error happened. Browser DevTools and Node inspect let you pause on breakpoints, step through code, and map minified bundles back to TypeScript with source maps.

blocks.text: When an **Error** is thrown, the JavaScript engine captures a **stack trace** — a list of function calls from the throw site up to the entry point. On V8 (Chrome and Node), it lives on the `stack` property as a multi-line string. Each line typically shows the function name, file, and line number. **Source maps** are separate files that map bundled/minified code back to original TypeScript so DevTools displays the correct lines. Without source maps, debugging production builds means reading one-letter variable names in line 1 of bundle.js.

entries.plainDefinition: Ordered list of call frames at the moment an error was created or thrown.
A debugger marker that pauses execution before a specific line runs.
entries.example: Click line 42 in Chrome Sources panel

entries.plainDefinition: JSON file linking compiled output lines to original source files for debugging.
JavaScript keyword that triggers a breakpoint when DevTools is open.
entries.example: debugger; // pauses here if inspector attached

blocks.text: Production incidents are won or lost on stack quality. Throwing strings erases frames. Wrapping without `cause` hides the root line. Source maps must ship to your error tracker (Sentry, Datadog) but not necessarily to public users — balance debuggability with exposing source. C# StackTrace on Exception is the same idea; both ecosystems punish `throw ex` / resetting stacks.

blocks.title: Stack is captured at creation time
blocks.body: new Error('x') captures stack when constructed, not when thrown. Reusing one Error object across throws can show a misleading origin — create a fresh Error per failure.

items.title: Reproduce with DevTools open
items.body: Chrome/Edge/Firefox Sources panel or Node --inspect / node inspect script.js.

items.title: Set breakpoints or use debugger
items.body: Pause before suspicious lines. Inspect locals, call stack, and scope chain.

items.title: Step over, into, out
items.body: F10 step over, F11 step into, Shift+F11 step out — same mental model as Visual Studio.

items.title: Enable source maps
items.body: DevTools Settings → enable JavaScript source maps. Build tools emit .map files alongside bundles.

items.title: Read the stack on failure
items.body: Console shows err.stack. Copy to error tracker with source map resolution for original filenames.

diagram.title: From throw to readable frame
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  THROW[throw new Error] --> V8[V8 captures stack frames]
  V8 --> BUNDLE[bundle.js line 1 col 9000]
  BUNDLE --> MAP[source map lookup]
  MAP --> TS[user.service.ts line 42]
  TS --> DEV[DevTools displays original file]

snippet.label: Reading and logging stack traces
snippet.explanation: Line 2: throw site appears at the top of the stack (below the message). Line 12: log stack in production — message alone loses call context.

snippet.label: debugger statement and conditional breakpoints
snippet.explanation: Line 3: debugger pauses only when inspector is attached. Line 7: --inspect-brk pauses on first line — useful for startup debugging.

snippet.label: Error.captureStackTrace (V8 / Node)
snippet.explanation: Line 6: Node/V8 API trims internal frames — similar to skipping infrastructure in C# stack traces. Not available in all browsers.

snippet.label: Source map comment in bundled output
snippet.explanation: Line 2: sourceMappingURL tells DevTools where to find the map. Line 5: enable in build config. Line 6: security — maps expose original source; restrict access in production.

blocks.title: Logging only err.message
blocks.body: Production alerts without stack cannot tell which code path failed. Always log stack (or use a library that serializes it).

blocks.title: Missing source maps in production
blocks.body: Stack points to bundle.js:1:40000. Upload maps to your monitoring tool even if you do not serve them publicly.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: Sentry release + source map upload resolves frames to original paths. V8 stack trace limit defaults to 10 frames — Error.stackTraceLimit = 50 for deep async chains. console.trace() prints current stack without throwing. Cross-realm errors (iframe) break instanceof and sometimes stack formatting. Node --enable-source-maps (stable in recent Node) applies maps without DevTools. Performance: collecting stack is relatively expensive — do not create Error in hot loops for control flow. C# PDB and JS source maps solve the same problem: symbolic debugging of optimized output.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain difference between message and stack. Never heard of source maps. Thinking minified production stacks are sufficient without maps. Saying throw new Error() and throw err reset stack the same way C# throw ex does.

interviewTakeaways: err.stack shows call frames; log it in production, not just message.
Source maps link bundles to TypeScript — upload to error trackers.
debugger and DevTools breakpoints mirror VS debugging.
60s: Stack on Error. Source maps for bundles. captureStackTrace in Node. throw same err preserves stack.
Follow-up: when is stack captured — at new Error or at throw?
commonPitfalls: Production logs with message only — no stack.
No source maps — unreadable bundle line numbers.
Strong answer: 'Error.stack at creation. Maps to TS in Sentry. captureStackTrace for clean library stacks. Never throw strings.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# StackTrace on Exception maps to compiled IL with PDB symbols. JavaScript uses source maps for the same debugging experience on transpiled code.
TypeScript sourceMap: true emits .js.map files. DevTools and Node --enable-source-maps consume them.
